title: Сделка на лестничной клетке  (The Deal on the Stairwell Landing)

segments.t: Out on the stairwell landing, Max hands Rodion Sergeyevich his coat and thanks him for playing along with their drunken karaoke act so that Nastya would be the one to send him away. The next day at Claude Monet, Chef Barinov tastes Max's vegetables and grudgingly praises them.
Если бы вы нам не подыграли, думаю.
Она из-за вас грозилась из дома уйти.
С вами приятно иметь дело, Максим Леонидович.
Ну и с работы тоже.
Слушайте, хорошее предложение.
Поедите на метро.
Вы сегодня отлично выглядите, шеф.
А твое какое дело?
И что ты здесь стоишь?
А ты что, там допьешь?
Зря вы с ним так, Виктор Петрович.
И без обид.
В вашем лице, Виктор Петрович.
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
Если бы вы нам не подыграли, думаю.
'If you had not played along with us, I think.' The plural past ending '-li' on the verb for 'to play along' covers a group or the polite 'you'.
Она из-за вас грозилась из дома уйти.
'Because of you, she was threatening to move out of the apartment.' Chef Viktor brings out the contrast between 'she' and 'because of' in a few short words. Vika answers right away.
С вами приятно иметь дело, Максим Леонидович.
'It is a pleasure doing business with you, Maxim Leonidovich.' The grammar packs 'with' and 'leonidovich' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
Ну и с работы тоже.
'And from work as well.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'come on' before landing on 'some'.
Слушайте, хорошее предложение.
'Listen, that is a very good offer.' The grammar packs 'listen' and 'offer' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Vika answers right away.
Поедите на метро.
'Take the metro instead.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'to eat' and finishing on 'metro'.
Вы сегодня отлично выглядите, шеф.
'You are looking great today, Chef.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'you' before landing on 'chef'.
А твое какое дело?
'And what business is it of yours?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'and' and finishing on 'matter'. Vika answers right away.
И что ты здесь стоишь?
'Why are you standing around here?' In Russian, the idea of 'both' flows naturally into 'stand' without extra filler words.
А ты что, там допьешь?
'Are you going to finish drinking that?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'and' before landing on 'to finish drinking'.
Зря вы с ним так, Виктор Петрович.
'You should not treat him like that, Viktor Petrovich.' Chef Viktor chooses the respectful plural 'you' alongside 'Petrovich' to keep a polite distance. Vika answers right away.
И без обид.
'And no hard feelings.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'both' before landing on 'hard feelings'.
В вашем лице, Виктор Петрович.
'In your person, Viktor Petrovich.' The grammar packs 'your' and 'Petrovich' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Let's hear the full exchange one more time at natural speed.
